title: Your Operating Model Wasn’t Built for AI. Neither Was Your Vendor’s.
summary: AI workflow automation can't fix a broken operating model. It amplifies it. Learn the Observe, Reconcile, Redesign framework for true operational transformation.
body_markdown:
From customer service and back-office support to finance, HR, and IT, companies are racing to scale AI based on a simple assumption: if AI can automate work, summarize knowledge, assist employees, and resolve issues faster, then businesses should move quickly… right?


If only it were that simple.


The problem is that most operating models were designed around people, processes, and systems that evolved over time. AI, on the other hand, relies on clarity. Clear data. Clear ownership. Clear decision-making. Clear workflows.


Without that clarity, the only thing AI does is automate the wrong things faster.


## The Opacity Problem: You Don’t Know What You Don’t Know


Ask five managers how a customer request moves through the organization, and there’s a good chance you’ll hear five versions of the same story.


Not because anyone is wrong, but because every organization has two versions of work:


- **The documented process** : what the organization believes happens.


- **The operational reality** : what people actually do to deliver outcomes every day.


The documented process is usually what gets mapped, measured, and shared with technology providers. It includes defined workflows, policies, roles, and expected handoffs.


Operational reality is different.


It’s the experience employees have built over years of navigating disconnected systems, changing priorities, customer expectations, and process gaps. It’s the judgment employees apply when policy and reality don’t fully align. It’s the knowledge that often lives with the people doing the work.


In many organizations, employees have become the connective tissue that holds the operation together. When AI is introduced, it highlights the difference between these two worlds:


- If knowledge is inconsistent, AI will deliver inconsistent answers.


- If workflows are fragmented, AI will expose those gaps.


- If ownership is unclear, AI will struggle to determine when to act, when to recommend, and when to escalate.


- If success metrics reward the wrong behaviors, AI may simply accelerate them.


That’s why[operational visibility](https://www.concentrix.com/services-solutions/operational-insights/) matters. Before organizations can redesign work for AI, they need to understand how work happens in everyday real-life scenarios.


## Capabilities Do Not Automatically Create Transformation


There is no shortage of[agentic AI](https://www.concentrix.com/services-solutions/agentic-ai/) technology available today.


BPOs, systems integrators, process intelligence platforms, and AI-native companies all bring valuable capabilities to the table. Many can help organizations automate tasks, improve efficiency, and scale operations. None of them, however, fix process opacity.


- **Legacy BPO/Outsourcers** operate on a model of absorbing back-office complexity and operating it more cost-effectively. The flaw is that they often digitize broken, manual, undocumented processes while relying on humans to handle exceptions. Promises of end-to-end intelligent operations can mask fragmented ownership, systems, and incentives without addressing what the process is, who owns outcomes, or why exceptions occur.


- **Global Systems Integrators** talk about reinvention but face the same challenge as BPOs: transformation requires an accurate view of how work is actually performed, including exceptions, workarounds, and undocumented decisions. They promise coordination across silos, yet executive architectures, process maps, and RACI charts often fail to reflect operational reality. The org chart may say one thing, but the workflow says another.


- **Process Intelligence & Discovery Vendors** often focus on agentic automation and orchestration. Their platforms encourage organizations to consider what can be automated rather than what should be redesigned. While process data reveals transaction paths, it rarely captures the judgment, workarounds, or incentives behind them. These vendors also promise AI agents embedded across enterprise workflows, but enabling every team to create agents doesn’t create a coherent operating model. It often spreads automation across even more silos.


- **AI-Native Challengers** position themselves as replacements for the BPO model, promising rapid results by connecting LLMs and AI agents to enterprise systems. The problem is that they sell tools rather than operational alignment and assume processes are already clean and structured. Applying AI agents to poorly understood workflows simply accelerates bad outcomes. Replacing humans with agents is a labor-cost shift, not an operating-model redesign, and it inherits the same policy complexity, exception handling, and broken upstream processes already in place.


Vendors, no matter what category they fall into, have useful technology and/or expertise. It’s why they’ve continued to remain relevant. Technology capability, however, isn’t the same as[operating-model readiness](https://www.concentrix.com/insights/thought-leadership/enterprise-ai-operating-model/) . The real risk is not buyingbad AI. It’s buying capable AI that scales the wrong operating logic.


## Before AI, Find Your Operational Truth


Before[scaling AI](https://www.concentrix.com/insights/blog/achieving-to-ai-at-scale/) , organizations need to uncover what we call their operational truth:


- The documented process is what the company says happens.


- The designed process is what leaders intended to happen.


- The operational truth is what actually happens.


These are not always the samething .


Finding operational truth requires looking beyond process maps and system data to understand how work gets done in practice. That starts with asking the right questions:


**Work Visibility:** Can you see work from beginning to end, including exceptions and informal workarounds?


- *What outcome is the process designed to achieve?*
- *Where does work really begin?*
- *Which systems, tools, spreadsheets, emails, and manual steps are involved?*


**Data and Knowledge Readiness:** Is the information AI will rely on accurate, accessible, current, and governed?


- *Where does critical data live?*
- *Which policies and procedures guide decisions?*
- *What knowledge exists only in people’s experience?*


**Decision Clarity:** Do you know where human judgment matters most?


- *Which decisions follow clear rules?*
- Which require context and discretion?
- *What drives exceptions and escalations?*


**Human-AI Accountability:** Who owns the outcome when AI acts, the human intervenes, or the workflow fails?


- *Who owns the end result?*
- *How are issues identified and resolved?*
- *What happens when intervention is needed?*


**Outcome Economics:** Are you measuring activity or impact?


- *What business problem are you trying to solve?*
- *Which metrics matter most: speed, quality, customer experience, risk, cost, or growth?*
- *What work should disappear altogether?*


The goal is not simply to automate tasks; it’s to[create better outcomes](https://www.concentrix.com/insights/blog/outcome-washing-pricing/) .


## The Path Forward: Rebuilding the Model Before Scaling Software


So far, we’ve explored what doesn’t work (and why), and you’velikely begun asking important questions about your operations. That’s where the path to self-discovery begins.


You don’t need to have every answer before starting your AI journey, but you do need a clear understanding of the work you want AI to support. A practical path forward often looks like this:


- **Observe** : Understand how work moves across people, systems, teams, and exceptions.


- **Reconcile** : Compare documented processes with operational reality and identify gaps, overlaps, and contradictions.


- **Redesign** : Simplify workflows, reduce unnecessary handoffs, clarify ownership, and remove friction before introducing automation.


- **Decide** : Determine which activities should be automated, augmented by AI, retained for human judgment, or eliminated altogether.


- **Orchestrate** : Connect people, systems, workflows, and AI into a coordinated operating model.


- **Govern** : Establish accountability, escalation paths, auditability, and clear performance expectations.


- **Improve** : Use operational data and employee feedback to continuously strengthen the model.


- **Measure** : Focus on outcomes that matter, not activity metrics that simply indicate technology adoption.


## Start With Your People (And What They Understand)


AI isn’t forcing organizations to change. It’s forcing them to see themselves clearly.


**3 Key Takeaways**


1. Understand reality before automating it.


2. Align people, processes, and AI around outcomes 3. Redesign the operating model before scaling the software.


3. Redesign the operating model before scaling the software.


For years, people have carried the weight of disconnected systems, unclear processes, and countless exceptions. AI doesn’t remove those realities. It exposes them.


Before investing in agents, automation, or outsourcing, organizations need to understand how work happens, who makes critical decisions, and what outcomes truly matter.


The companies that succeed with AI won’t be the ones that automate the fastest. They’ll be the ones that understand their operations deeply enough to redesign them first.


Because the future of operations won’t be built by automating yesterday’s work.[It will be built by finally understanding it](https://www.concentrix.com/newrealities/) .
